title: How MCP authorization works, and the issuer check that stops token theft
summary: How an MCP client finds its OAuth server, how a flaw in the official Python SDK leaked codes and PKCE verifiers, and the two issuer checks that stop it.

html:
The short version An MCP client learns where to sign in from the MCP server it is about to call, so a hostile server can point it at the wrong place. The defence is the issuer check: the authorization server metadata must name exactly the issuer the client asked for, and the authorization response must come back with that same issuer. Upgrade the official SDKs, and pin the issuer for machine-to-machine clients.

On 28 September 2026 the maintainers of the official MCP (Model Context Protocol) Python SDK published advisory GHSA-qx49-fqc8-xw99. A malicious MCP server could make an SDK client send its OAuth client secret, authorization code and PKCE code verifier to a token endpoint the attacker controlled. The fixed releases had shipped three weeks earlier, on 7 September, and the TypeScript SDK published a matching advisory on 30 September. If you connect AI agents to remote tools, this is worth fifteen minutes of your time.

This post walks through how MCP authorization works in the current specification (version 2026-07-28), where the gap was, and the two checks that close it.

1Know who plays which role

MCP authorization is plain OAuth 2.1 with a few extra rules. Three parties are involved:

  • The MCP server is an OAuth resource server. It holds the tools and data, and it accepts access tokens.

  • The authorization server signs the user in and issues tokens. It can run next to the MCP server or be a separate identity provider (IdP) such as your company login.

  • The MCP client, usually an AI agent or IDE, is the OAuth client. It gets a token and sends it on every request.

Authorization only applies to HTTP transports. Local servers that run over stdio should take credentials from the environment instead, so this post does not apply to them.

2Follow how the client finds the authorization server

The client starts knowing only the MCP server URL. It discovers everything else from documents the MCP server and authorization server publish.

First, the client calls the MCP server without a token. The server answers 401 and points to its protected resource metadata, defined in RFC 9728:

HTTPHTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource",
                         scope="files:read"

If the header is missing, the client tries two well-known addresses on the MCP server, the path-specific one first, then /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource at the root. If neither exists, the specification says to stop or use pre-configured values.

The metadata document must list at least one authorization server:

JSON{
  "resource": "https://mcp.example.com",
  "authorization_servers": ["https://auth.example.com"],
  "scopes_supported": ["files:read"]
}

The client then fetches that authorization server's own metadata (RFC 8414). For an issuer with no path it tries /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server first and /.well-known/openid-configuration second. That metadata says where the login page and the token endpoint are.

Notice the trust problem. The MCP server chose which authorization server the client talks to, and the metadata chose where the token endpoint is. If either answer is forged, the client sends its secrets to the wrong place.

3Apply the issuer check to every metadata document

RFC 8414 section 3.3 has a simple rule. The issuer value inside the metadata must be identical to the issuer the client used to build the metadata URL. If it differs, the client must not use the document. The 2026-07-28 MCP specification now spells this out, with an example: metadata fetched from attacker.example that claims "issuer": "https://honest.example" must be rejected.

Here is the check in a few lines of Python. The specification also requires PKCE with the S256 method, so the client refuses metadata that does not advertise it:

Pythonfrom urllib.parse import urlsplit

def metadata_url(issuer: str) -> str:
    """RFC 8414 section 3.1: put the well-known suffix between the host and the path."""
    parts = urlsplit(issuer)
    return f"{parts.scheme}://{parts.netloc}/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server{parts.path.rstrip('/')}"

def check_metadata(expected_issuer: str, metadata: dict) -> dict:
    """RFC 8414 section 3.3: the document must name exactly the issuer we asked about."""
    if metadata.get("issuer") != expected_issuer:
        raise ValueError(f"issuer mismatch: {metadata.get('issuer')!r} != {expected_issuer!r}")
    if "S256" not in metadata.get("code_challenge_methods_supported", []):
        raise ValueError("authorization server does not advertise PKCE S256")
    return metadata

The comparison is a plain string comparison. Do not lowercase, trim a trailing slash or otherwise normalise either value first; https://auth.example.com and https://auth.example.com/ are different issuers.

4See how the Python SDK skipped the check

The SDK did validate the issuer on its main path, but not on every path. The advisory names two gaps in the 2.x line: the legacy fallback for servers that publish no protected resource metadata, and the step-up path after a 403 insufficient_scope response. In the 1.x line the check was missing on every path. Separately, stored client credentials were not tied to the authorization server that issued them.

The legacy fallback dates from the first MCP authorization specification (2025-03-26). It treated the MCP server's own origin as the authorization server and even defined default /authorize, /token and /register paths when metadata was missing. Later versions removed that idea, but the SDKs kept a fallback for older servers.

A malicious server could use that path like this:

  1. Publish no protected resource metadata, so the client falls back to asking the MCP server itself for authorization server metadata.

  2. Serve metadata whose login page belongs to the victim's real identity provider, but whose token endpoint belongs to the attacker.

  3. The user signs in on the genuine login page, so nothing looks wrong.

  4. The client sends the authorization code, the PKCE code verifier and its client secret to the attacker's token endpoint.

  5. The attacker redeems them at the real identity provider and receives a valid access token.

PKCE did not help. It stops someone who steals the code alone, but here the client handed over the verifier too. The MCP security guidance says it directly: PKCE alone fails because the client "transmits the code_verifier to the attacker's token endpoint".

The advisory scores the flaw 7.5 (High) for the two machine-to-machine providers, which need no user present, and 6.5 for the interactive provider, where a person has to start the sign-in. It has no CVE number.

5Add the second check: the issuer in the authorization response

The 2026-07-28 specification adds a second line of defence from RFC 9207. Before sending the user to sign in, the client records the issuer from the validated metadata, next to its PKCE verifier and state. Authorization servers should return an iss parameter with the authorization code. The client must compare it before sending the code to any token endpoint:

Pythondef check_callback(expected_issuer: str, metadata: dict, params: dict) -> str:
    """RFC 9207 section 2.4: compare iss before the code goes to any token endpoint."""
    iss = params.get("iss")
    if iss is None and metadata.get("authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported"):
        raise ValueError("iss missing from the authorization response")
    if iss is not None and iss != expected_issuer:
        raise ValueError(f"authorization response from the wrong issuer: {iss!r}")
    return params["code"]

The rules are:

  • If iss is present, it must match the recorded issuer exactly.

  • If the server advertises authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported and iss is missing, reject the response.

  • If the server does not advertise it and sends no iss, continue. A future revision is expected to make iss mandatory for servers.

This check is only as good as the recorded issuer. If the client recorded an issuer from metadata it never validated, comparing against it proves nothing, which is why step 3 comes first.

6Fix your stack today

Upgrade the SDK. For Python, the fixed versions are mcp 1.30.0 on the 1.x line and 2.2.0 on the 2.x line. Affected versions are 1.9.1 to 1.29.1 and every 2.x release before 2.2.0. For TypeScript, the fixes are @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.31.0 and @modelcontextprotocol/client 2.2.0.

Bashpip install --upgrade "mcp>=2.2.0"     # or "mcp>=1.30.0,<2" if you stay on 1.x

Pin the issuer on machine-to-machine clients. Upgrading is not enough for ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider and PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider. Without an issuer, they still send credentials to whichever authorization server the MCP server names. Leaving it out now raises a deprecation warning, and it becomes required in version 3.0. In TypeScript, the bundled providers need the expectedIssuer option.

Pythonimport os
from mcp.client.auth.extensions.client_credentials import ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider

auth = ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider(
    server_url="https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
    storage=token_storage,                       # your TokenStorage implementation
    client_id="reporting-agent",
    client_secret=os.environ["MCP_CLIENT_SECRET"],
    issuer="https://auth.example.com",           # pin the authorization server
)

Clean up old state. Clear stored client registrations that were saved without an issuer, which includes everything 1.x stored before 1.30.0. If a client may have connected to an untrusted server, rotate its client secret and revoke its tokens at the authorization server.

Check the server side too. The specification requires MCP servers to accept only tokens issued for them as the audience, and they "MUST NOT accept or transit any other tokens". Clients must send the RFC 8707 resource parameter with the MCP server's canonical URI in both the authorization and token requests, so tokens are bound to one server. The Python fixes also added a server option, validate_token_resource, to enforce the audience.

MCP servers built with the SDK, stdio clients and clients that attach their own tokens were not affected by this advisory.

Common mistakesNormalising issuers before comparing them, so a trailing slash or case change slips through. Taking the expected issuer from the same metadata you are trying to validate. Assuming the upgrade alone protects client-credentials and private-key JWT clients without issuer=. Running tests with deprecation warnings hidden: on 1.30.0 the missing-issuer warning is a DeprecationWarning, which Python hides by default.

What the issuer check does not cover

The issuer check stops a server from borrowing someone else's identity provider. It does not make every MCP server trustworthy:

  • A server with its own authorization server. A hostile server can run a real authorization server under its own name and pass every check. Decide which servers your agents may connect to, and keep scopes small.

  • Tool poisoning and prompt injection. A server that authenticates correctly can still return harmful tool descriptions or content.

  • Weak registration. Dynamic Client Registration is deprecated in the 2026-07-28 specification in favour of Client ID Metadata Documents, because self-registered clients can claim any name on the consent screen.

OAuth 2.1 itself is still an IETF draft, and the MCP specification keeps tightening these rules release by release. The lesson from this flaw is broader than MCP: a security check that runs only on the happy path will eventually be missing on the path an attacker chooses.
